structured_output.hypothesis: Far more plant taxa native to Europe are naturalised in the La Plata region (Argentina and Uruguay) and in Australia than taxa native exclusively to the southern hemisphere are naturalised in Europe, where such taxa are extremely few.
structured_output.pass_criterion: Let A = number of taxa native to Europe and naturalised in Argentina or Uruguay (La Plata), B = number of taxa native to Europe and naturalised in Australia, and C = number of taxa with native range wholly in the southern hemisphere (Australasia, South America, southern Africa) and naturalised in at least one European region. The claim passes if A ≥ 100, B ≥ 100 with A > B, and C/A ≤ 0.10 (also C/B ≤ 0.10, with C ≤ 150 in absolute terms, counting "extremely few" as at most that).
structured_output.fail_criterion: The claim fails if C/A > 0.25 or C/B > 0.25, or if A < 50, or if B ≥ A, which would contradict "in a lesser degree in Australia". Results between these bounds (0.10 < ratio ≤ 0.25) count as inconclusive and the claim is not confirmed.
structured_output.interpretation: "European productions cover the ground... have beaten the natives" is measured only as naturalisation (taxa recorded as established in the wild). GloNAF does not record displacement of natives, so that part is not tested. "La Plata" is mapped to the GloNAF regions Argentina and Uruguay. "Southern forms" is mapped to taxa whose native range lies wholly in the southern hemisphere (Australasia, South America, southern Africa). "Any part of Europe" is mapped to all GloNAF regions in Europe. Native ranges would come from the WCVP-linked taxon table (glonaf_taxon_wcvp.csv) or, if not given there, from a WCVP lookup on the taxon names. Naturalised taxon counts are a modern proxy for Darwin's impression of how common and abundant these species are. The dataset describes today, which matches his "at the present day". One caveat is that taxon counts per region are affected by uneven survey effort. A further caveat is that Australian plants such as Acacia and Eucalyptus are now known to be widely naturalised in southern Europe, so the claim could fail on modern data.

dataset.name: Global Naturalized Alien Flora (GloNAF). Open access data to support research on understanding global plant invasions.
dataset.publisher: Zenodo (GloNAF project; data manager Amy J.S. Davis, with van Kleunen, Pyšek, Essl, Kreft, Weigelt, Winter and others)
dataset.why_it_fits: It lists the vascular plant taxa naturalised in each world region, so naturalised taxa can be counted for Argentina, Uruguay, Australia and European regions. Files: glonaf_TxR.csv (taxon-by-region records), glonaf_region.csv (region names and continents), glonaf_taxon_wcvp.csv (taxon names matched to WCVP, from which native ranges can be taken or looked up) and glonaf_flora2.csv. Fields used: region, taxon and native-range fields, with the data dictionaries for field definitions.
